The **[Mexico City Metro](Mexico_City_Metro "Mexico City Metro")** is the largest and busiest heavy-rail rapid transit system in Mexico and [second in North America](List_of_North_American_rapid_transit_systems_by_ridership "List of North American rapid transit systems by ridership"), only behind the [New York City Subway](New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway").

As of 2014, the system is composed of 12 lines denominated 1 through 9, 12, A and B, totalling 226.5 km (140.7 mi) of track length and 195 stations. Of all stations, 115 are underground (either in shallow box-tunnels or deep circular tunnels), 54 are at street-level and 26 are elevated.

## Line 1: Observatorio – Pantitlán

Main article: [Mexico City Metro Line 1](Mexico_City_Metro_Line_1 "Mexico City Metro Line 1")

Line 1's Chapultepec - Zaragoza section was the first of the system to be opened, on September 4, 1969. The line was brought to its current length on August 22, 1984 with its final extension from Zaragoza to Pantitlán.

Line 1 runs mostly in a shallow box-tunnel just a few meters below the street, except for its initial stretch from [Observatorio](Observatorio_metro_station "Observatorio metro station") to [Tacubaya](Tacubaya_metro_station "Tacubaya metro station"), where it starts at street-level and progressively goes down to a deep circular tunnel through Tacubaya, where the box-tunnel begins. Line 1 is served by MP-68, NM-83 and NE-92 trains, built in France, Mexico and Spain in 1968, 1983 and 1992, respectively.

Transfer with other Metro lines is available at Tacubaya (lines 7 & 9), Balderas (line 3), Salto del Agua (Line 8), Pino Suárez (line 2), Candelaria (line 4), San Lázaro (line B) and Pantitlán (lines 5, 9 & A). Transfer to the [Metrobús](Mexico_City_Metrob%C3%BAs "Mexico City Metrobús") bus rapid transit (BRT) system is available at Tacubaya (line 2), Insurgentes (line 1), Cuauhtémoc (line 3), Balderas (line 3), Pino Suárez (line 4) and San Lázaro (lines 4 & 5).

## Line 2: Cuatro Caminos – Tasqueña

Main article: [Mexico City Metro Line 2](Mexico_City_Metro_Line_2 "Mexico City Metro Line 2")

[Line 2](Mexico_City_Metro_Line_2 "Mexico City Metro Line 2") was the second line in the system to open, in 1970. After two expansions, the line has 24 stations over a total track length of 23.431 km (14.559 mi), of which 20.713 km (12.870 mi) are passenger track. The line has a general northwest–south direction passing through the city center and its color is [blue](Blue "Blue"). It starts at the border of the Federal District and the [State of Mexico](State_of_Mexico "State of Mexico") and ends in the city south.

It commutes with line 7 at [Tacuba](Tacuba_metro_station "Tacuba metro station"), line 3 at [Hidalgo](Hidalgo_metro_station "Hidalgo metro station"), line 8 at [Bellas Artes](Bellas_Artes_metro_station_(Mexico_City) "Bellas Artes metro station (Mexico City)"), line 1 at [Pino Suárez](Pino_Su%C3%A1rez_metro_station "Pino Suárez metro station"), lines 8 and 9 at [Chabacano](Chabacano_metro_station "Chabacano metro station") and line 12 at [Ermita](Ermita_metro_station "Ermita metro station"). At Tasqueña it links with the [Mexico City Light Rail](Mexico_City_Light_Rail "Mexico City Light Rail") to <Xochimilco>. It used to be served by NC-82 and some NM-83 trains.

Line 2 was the scene of the worst accident in the Mexico City Metro's history on October 20, 1975, when a crash occurred between two trains at Viaducto Station. One train was parked at the station picking up passengers when it was hit by another train that did not stop in time. Twenty people were killed and several wounded. After that accident, automatic traffic lights were installed in all the lines.

Thirteen stations run underground while the remaining ten are surface stations. The line is currently served by NM-02 trains built in Mexico in 2004.

The first section of [line 3](Mexico_City_Metro_Line_3 "Mexico City Metro Line 3") was opened in 1970. ## History

The *Subte* opened in 1913, becoming the 13th underground system in the world,[[4]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-New_York_Times_Burgeoise-4) as well as the first in [Latin America](Latin_America "Latin America"), the [Southern Hemisphere](Southern_Hemisphere "Southern Hemisphere") and the <Hispanophone> world,[[5]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-ambito.com-5) followed by the [Madrid Metro](Madrid_Metro "Madrid Metro") in 1919.[[6]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-Perfil-6)[[7]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-7) The network was originally built and operated by three separate private companies and later nationalised in 1939. In 1952 it was absorbed by a unified state administration, in 1963 it became the property of a newly founded company, which changed hands in 1979.[[8]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-Ricardo2015-82-8) The Subte then entered into a [concession](Concession_(contract) "Concession (contract)") model in the mid-1990s through which private sector parties were to submit bids to execute investment plans "designed and funded" by the state, while implemented by the concessionaire. All the Underground lines, along with the [Urquiza Line](Urquiza_Line "Urquiza Line") and [Premetro](Premetro_(Buenos_Aires) "Premetro (Buenos Aires)") were offered as 20-year concessions to interested private parties. By 1995, Metrovías took over the Subte under a $395 million plan.[[9]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-Plant2007-9)

### Early days

See also: [Line A (Buenos Aires Underground)](Line_A_(Buenos_Aires_Underground) "Line A (Buenos Aires Underground)") and [Trams in Buenos Aires](Trams_in_Buenos_Aires "Trams in Buenos Aires")

Discussions on the need to build an underground transportation system in Buenos Aires began in the late nineteenth century, alongside the [tramway system](Trams_in_Buenos_Aires "Trams in Buenos Aires"), which was one of the most extensive in the world at the time. The first trams appeared in 1870, and by about 1900 the system was in a crisis exacerbated by the monopolisation of the lines, which had concentrated under the ownership of fewer companies during the [electrification](Electrification "Electrification") of the system.[[10]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-AAT-10)

In this context, the first proposals for the building of an underground system were made, along with requests for government grants: first, in 1886, and several more in 1889. However, the [Ministry of Interior](Interior_ministry "Interior ministry") (*Ministerio del Interior*, in Spanish) denied the city administration the power to license building in the city's [subsoil](Subsoil "Subsoil") and for this reason, subsequent drafts were submitted directly to this ministry.[[11]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-11) In 1894, when it was decided to construct the [Congress](Argentine_National_Congress "Argentine National Congress") building in its present location, the underground idea was revived, since it would shorten the travel time between the [Casa Rosada](Casa_Rosada "Casa Rosada") and the Congress. In 1896 Miguel Cané, former Mayor of Buenos Aires (1892–1893), expressed the need to build an underground railway similar to the one in London[[12]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-Tejera-12)[[13]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-ladm-13)

There were numerous proposals at the time to build an electric [aerial tramway](Aerial_tramway "Aerial tramway"), with one such line to go down the [Avenida de Mayo](Avenida_de_Mayo "Avenida de Mayo").[[13]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-ladm-13)[[14]](Buenos_Aires_Underground#cite_note-Singh-14) One proposal was the 1889 *Le Tellier* proposal, which envisioned multiple lines running along the city's wider avenues with the trams [moved using cables](Cable_car_(railway) "Cable car (railway)") and would hang from steel rails fixed to 6-metre-high (20 ft) steel and iron posts positioned in 10-to-15-metre (33 to 49 ft) intervals.
